source.title: Do Highly Over-Parameterized Neural Networks Generalize Since Bad Solutions are Rare?

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether zero-training-error solutions tend to generalize, using random sampling of network weights and measured test errors. It does not apply the random-label or unstructured-input interventions in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The introduction mentions random-label memorization as prior work [4]; that is not a result of this study. Its experiments measure true-label generalization among zero-training-error solutions.
record.test_reason: The study measures generalization among uniformly sampled weights conditioned on zero training error on true-label tasks. It does not test random-label fitting, corrupted-label learning, unstructured inputs, or regularizer removal. Random-label memorization is cited as background; Figure 1B illustrates chance population error under independent random labels without testing whether training fits them.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors prove conditional bounds on the fraction of bad interpolating solutions, validate them in their sampled settings, and propose this as an explanation for generalization without explicit regularization. They acknowledge that SGD does not sample minima uniformly and that sampling restricts their experiments to small training sets.
record.recipe_differences: The study samples weights uniformly to estimate the distribution of zero-training-error solutions; it does not reproduce random-label memorization training. Its Caltech101 SGD result is adapted from cited prior work.
record.method_sensitivity: The ten-hidden-layer synthetic network converges more slowly than the shallower networks, and the study reports a positive correlation for some training-set sizes in that network. On Caltech101, VGG19 has better results than ResNet18.

fits_no_version.finding: For the two shallow synthetic networks at n=30, approximately three quarters of sampled interpolating solutions have test error below 0.2. The deeper network's distribution improves more slowly with sample size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: True-label generalization among uniformly sampled interpolating weights depends on architecture and training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: For both MNIST architectures at n=24, about 75% of sampled zero-training-error solutions have test error below 0.2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many uniformly sampled interpolating solutions generalize on the tested MNIST binary task.

fits_no_version.finding: On Caltech101, sampled VGG19 interpolating solutions average 75% test accuracy with 10 training examples per class; ResNet18 performs worse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization of randomly sampled interpolating solutions varies across architectures on this true-label task.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: Random-sampling experiments are limited to relatively small settings because finding zero-training-error solutions becomes time-consuming as sample size grows. The paper notes that SGD need not converge to global minima with equal probability. The ResNet18 accuracy comparison is not numerically stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Figure-only intermediate values and precise variances were not transcribed because the text does not state them.

untested.parts: SGD fitting completely random training labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between real and random labels and convergence versus corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across label-corruption fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting, and effects of removing them on true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noise and differences in real-label versus random-label learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: Zero training error is a selection condition in these experiments, not evidence that SGD learns random labels. Likewise, random sampling of weights is distinct from randomizing labels or inputs.

versions.untested_parts: No random labeling, chance test error under random labels, or unchanged-hyperparameter comparison is tested.
No training-time comparison or corruption-fraction convergence sweep.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
No sweep of random label-corruption fractions.
No comparison of regularizers or data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
No measurement of learning order or comparison of real and random labels over training.

rows.subject: MLP with one hidden layer, 10 hidden units
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on synthetic two-Gaussian classification; measured test errors at n=30.
rows.measure: Fraction of sampled zero-training-error solutions with test error below 0.2; average test error also compared with the theoretical bound.
rows.uncertainty: In only one of the 1,000 trials there is a test error slightly above 0.4.
rows.note: True-label generalization among randomly sampled training-error-zero solutions; not a random-label experiment.
rows.check: Measures true-label generalization after selecting zero-training-error weights, not any claim version. The text says more than 75% have error below 0.2; its accompanying notation uses epsilon=0.2 despite defining the threshold elsewhere as Emin+epsilon.

rows.subject: MLP with one hidden layer, 100 hidden units
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on synthetic two-Gaussian classification; measured test errors at n=30.
rows.measure: Fraction of sampled zero-training-error solutions with test error below 0.2; test errors compared with the smaller network.
rows.baseline: Network with 10 hidden units; its corresponding result is described as about 75% below 0.2.
rows.value: About 75% of cases had test error below 0.2; none of the 1,000 trials had test error above 0.4.
rows.note: Authors describe the test-error distribution as more or less identical to that of the ten-times-smaller network.
rows.check: Measures true-label generalization among sampled interpolating weights, not random-label fitting.

rows.subject: MLP with ten hidden layers, ten units each
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on synthetic two-Gaussian classification; measured test errors across training-set sizes.
rows.measure: Distribution of test errors among training-error-zero solutions and comparison of mean test error with the bound.
rows.value: The distribution converges more slowly; the peak of D(E) resolves with increasing n. The bound is valid, but for some n there is a positive correlation between ϕε(S) and ω(S).
rows.note: Sampling was stopped at n = 22 because finding zero-training-error solutions became too time-consuming.
rows.check: Slower change in the test-error distribution with sample size is not slower optimization or noise memorization over training. No claim-relative partial effect is measured.

rows.subject: Network with two leaky output ReLUs and no hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on MNIST digits 1 and 2; measured test errors across training-set sizes.

conditions.value: in both scenarios, n = 24 is discussed

rows.measure: Test errors among training-error-zero solutions and comparison of mean errors with the bound.
rows.value: For both MNIST scenarios, at n = 24 about 75% of test errors are below 0.2; the bound holds and equality is reported.
rows.note: The stated about-75% result is reported jointly for the two MNIST scenarios and is not separately attributed to this architecture.
rows.check: Measures true-label generalization under random weight sampling. The approximately 75% result is explicitly stated for both MNIST networks.

rows.subject: One-hidden-layer MLP with 10 hidden leaky ReLUs and two leaky output ReLUs
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on MNIST digits 1 and 2; measured test errors across training-set sizes.

conditions.value: in both scenarios, n = 24 is discussed

rows.measure: Test errors among training-error-zero solutions and comparison of mean errors with the bound.
rows.value: For both MNIST scenarios, at n = 24 about 75% of test errors are below 0.2; the bound holds and equality is reported.
rows.note: The stated about-75% result is reported jointly for the two MNIST scenarios and is not separately attributed to this architecture.
rows.check: Measures true-label generalization under random weight sampling. No regularizer-removal comparison or random-label experiment is reported.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on Caltech101 airplane and motorcycle classification; measured test accuracy.
rows.measure: Mean test accuracy of randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions.
rows.value: At n = 10 the mean test accuracy is 75%.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5B shows variances; no numeric variance is stated in text.
rows.note: Authors say a rough extrapolation to n = 20 leads to the range of VGG19 in Figure 5A; the n = 20 value is not separately recorded as a measured result.
rows.check: The 75% accuracy is for sampled interpolating weights with 10 training samples per class, not SGD fitting random labels.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions on Caltech101 airplane and motorcycle classification; measured test accuracy.
rows.measure: Mean test accuracy of randomly sampled zero-training-error solutions.
rows.baseline: VGG19, reported as better than ResNet18 in the experiment.
rows.value: The text says ResNet18 is worse than VGG19; precise mean values are shown in Figure 5B only.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5B shows variances; no numeric variance is stated in text.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison but does not state a numeric accuracy for ResNet18.
rows.check: The architecture comparison concerns true-label generalization under random sampling. Worse accuracy than VGG19 does not constitute a partial effect for any listed version.

rows.subject: VGG19
rows.operation_detail: Stochastic gradient descent trained the network to zero training error without regularization; this is a cited prior experiment adapted in Figure 5A.

conditions.value: 20 examples from each class; also 200 training data discussed

rows.value: 95% accuracy with 20 examples from each class; with 200 training data the test accuracy is almost 100%.
rows.note: This is identified as results shown in [7] and adapted in Figure 5A, not an experiment newly run in this study.
rows.check: Exclude as this study's result: Figure 5A and its SGD accuracies are adapted from reference [7]. Although relevant to generalization without explicit regularization, these are cited results, not this study's own regularizer-removal experiment.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
